common_name: Jellicorse White Dent Corn (Jellicorse Twin Dent, Tennessee Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 short rows for reliable wind pollination once soil has warmed well past last frost.

directions: Jellicorse is a white-cobbed, 12-to-14-row dent corn selected by farmer Reginald Jellicorse of Elmwood, Tennessee in the 1910s, descended from Tennessee Red Cob and Tuscarora White lines; the Tennessee Experiment Station trialed it from 1919-1923 and clocked it second only to Neal's Paymaster for yield while noting it consistently set two ears per stalk even on poor, under-fertilized ground. Its deep Southern pedigree translates to genuine tolerance for the brutal heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer, where many Midwestern dent corns stall out or fail to pollinate. Sow into warm soil in blocks rather than single rows, keep moisture steady through silking, and let the ears dry down fully on the stalk before shelling for cornmeal, grits, or hominy. Save the best double-eared stalks for next year's seed to keep the twin-ear trait strong.
sources: USDA National Plant Germplasm System (GRIN, PI Ames 3004)

common_name: Neal's Paymaster Corn (Tennessee Two-Eared Heirloom Dent Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks after soil is reliably warm; this variety's tall stalks and double-ear habit reward deep, fertile soil and a full-length warm season.

directions: Bred by farmer William Haskell Neal of Wilson County, Tennessee, beginning his field selection in 1898 and introducing seed to neighbors by 1912, Neal's Paymaster was the first reliably two-ears-per-stalk dent corn, with white kernels on a distinctive red cob and towering 9-10-foot stalks; by 1937 it reportedly accounted for roughly a third of Tennessee's entire corn crop, prized for shrugging off heat and marginal soil that defeated other field corns of the day. Plant it in blocks for wind pollination, give it a full season of warmth and moisture, and expect genuinely heavy yields per stalk thanks to the twin ears. This is a field (not sweet) corn grown to dry for cornmeal, grits, hominy, or livestock feed, so let ears cure fully on the stalk before shelling and storing.
sources: Main Street Media of Tennessee, Cheatham County Exchange

common_name: Jarvis Golden Prolific Corn (Southern Heirloom Yellow Dent Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows well after last frost; needs its full 110+ day season of Gulf South heat to dry down properly.

directions: Registered around 1930, Jarvis Golden Prolific was once a widely grown open-pollinated Southern field corn, known for its sizeable 10-inch yellow dent ears on comparatively shorter 6-to-8-foot stalks. Give it full sun, block plantings for wind pollination, and consistent moisture through tasseling and silking, which matter more in Gulf Coast humidity than drought stress does. Because it runs a longer season than modern hybrids, start it as soon as the soil is reliably warm in spring to give it time to mature before the latest, most brutal stretch of late-summer heat. Dry ears fully on the stalk and shell for cornmeal, grits, or chicken and livestock feed.
sources: The Historic Foodie (heirloom corn variety survey)

common_name: Texas Pinkeye Purple Hull Pea (Texas A&M Bush Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil is reliably above 65°F; this tall, upright bush type was bred for mechanical harvest but shells easily by hand in the home garden too.

directions: Developed by the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station as a canning-industry selection, Texas Pinkeye Purple Hull is a tall, erect bush-type southern pea bred for once-over mechanical harvest, but it performs just as well picked by hand through a long Gulf Coast summer. Pods are green-and-purple when immature and deepen to full purple at maturity, shelling out cream-colored peas with the classic bright pink eye in as little as 55 days. Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil; like other cowpeas it fixes its own nitrogen, so skip heavy fertilizing and keep watering light once plants are established. Succession sow every 2-3 weeks through midsummer for a steady supply of fresh shelling peas ahead of fall frost.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture (FSA-6102)

common_name: Floribibb Lettuce (University of Florida Heat-Tolerant Bibb Lettuce)

planting.note: Best sown in fall through early spring along the Gulf Coast, where Floribibb's heat tolerance stretches the harvest window well past when ordinary bibb types would bolt and turn bitter.

directions: Bred at the University of Florida's lettuce program at the Everglades Research and Education Center specifically for the state's warm, humid growing seasons, Floribibb is a gourmet butterhead with soft, buttery rosettes and bred-in resistance to two common lettuce viruses that otherwise thrive in hot, muggy weather. Direct sow or transplant small starts 8-10 inches apart in loose, moisture-retentive soil, and keep it out of the most intense afternoon sun once temperatures climb, since it tolerates heat far better than it tolerates drought or deep shade. Along the Gulf Coast this is a cool-season crop best grown fall through early spring rather than through summer; harvest whole heads or outer leaves once rosettes fill out, generally 55-65 days from seed.

planting.note: Needs a long, hot season and generous room to ramble; give hills 6 feet or more of space and a sturdy season of heat to size fruit up fully.

directions: A traditional Caribbean calabaza landrace long grown in Cuba and across the Gulf South, Cuban Neck produces a massive crookneck fruit with a slender, nearly all-flesh neck and a bulbous seed cavity at the blossom end, typically running 7-15 pounds at full size and colored in a mottled patchwork of orange, green, tan, and white that fades toward solid tan in storage. The dense, deep-orange flesh is sweeter and more aromatic than a supermarket butternut, with higher sugar and dry matter, and the long solid neck makes it especially easy to peel and cube for savory Creole and Caribbean cooking. Give vines full sun and a long, humid growing season — this is one of the most heat- and mildew-tolerant winter squashes available, bred by generations of tropical gardeners rather than temperate breeding programs. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists a thumbnail, then cure in a warm, airy spot for a week before moving to cool storage.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension (HS572, Calabaza)

common_name: La Estrella Calabaza (University of Florida Gulf Coast-Adapted Tropical Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills once soil is warm; matures noticeably faster than old-style vining calabaza landraces, a real advantage in gardens with a shorter frost-free window.

directions: Developed by University of Florida breeders specifically for Gulf Coast and Caribbean growing conditions, La Estrella is a medium-vine calabaza selected to flower and fruit earlier than the extra-long-vine landrace types traditionally grown further south, making it a better fit for home gardens with limited trellis or ground space. Fruits run boxy to round, averaging 6-10 pounds, with a mottled green-and-tan waxy rind and dense, vividly orange, nutty-flavored flesh that is unusually heavy for its size. Direct sow into warm soil in full sun, keep moisture even through fruit set, and expect a noticeably shorter season to harvest than old heirloom calabaza vines. Let fruit fully harden on the vine, cure briefly in a warm spot, and store in a cool, dry location for use in soups, stews, and Caribbean and Creole-style savory dishes through winter.
